The best way to understand "abstract" is to start with its opposite: concrete. A concrete thing is something real, physical, and tangible — something you can experience directly through your senses. A dog is concrete. A chair is concrete. Rain, fire, a apple, a broken bone — all concrete. You can touch them, see them, smell them, or hear them. They exist out there in the physical world, independent of your thoughts.

An abstract thing, by contrast, exists only as an idea or concept in the mind. It has no physical form. You cannot hold it, see it, or point to it directly. Think of words like love, justice, freedom, courage, democracy, beauty, time, truth, evil, infinity. These things are genuinely real and meaningful — but they don't exist as physical objects. You can see a person acting bravely, but you cannot see "courage" itself floating around in the room. You can observe a fair trial, but you cannot touch "justice." The concept lives in thought and language, not in the physical world.

This is the heart of the word: abstract = existing in thought, not in physical reality.
The Spectrum from Concrete to Abstract

One of the most important things to understand is that "abstract" is not a simple yes-or-no category. It is a spectrum, and you can move along it in degrees.

Consider this chain: Labrador → dog → animal → living thing → existence. Each step moves you further from the concrete and deeper into the abstract. "Labrador" is very concrete — you can picture a specific animal. "Dog" is slightly more general. "Animal" is even broader. "Living thing" is broader still. And "existence" is so general and removed from any specific physical thing that it is highly abstract. As you move up the chain, you strip away more and more specific, physical details and deal increasingly with pure concepts.

This is why abstract ideas are often harder to define than concrete ones. If someone asks "what is a chair?" you can simply point to one. If someone asks "what is justice?" you cannot point — you have to think, reason, and use other words to explain it. That difficulty is a signature of abstraction.
Degrees of Abstraction in Everyday Life

You encounter abstract and concrete things constantly, often without noticing the difference.

The number "5" is abstract. You can have 5 apples (concrete), 5 people (concrete), 5 seconds (somewhat abstract), but the number 5 itself — as a pure mathematical concept — has no physical form. Mathematics is almost entirely abstract, which is part of why children often find it difficult: they are being asked to work with pure ideas before they have enough experience with physical examples.

Emotions are abstract. You can see the physical signs of someone being angry — a flushed face, a raised voice, clenched fists — but "anger" itself, as a feeling and a concept, is abstract. It lives in the inner world of experience and mind.

Moral and social concepts are heavily abstract: rights, responsibility, fairness, dignity, guilt, honour. These concepts shape human society enormously, yet none of them are physical things. You cannot weigh "honour" on a scale.

Time is interestingly abstract. You can see a clock (concrete), but time itself — the concept of duration, of past and future — is abstract. Philosophers and physicists have argued about its true nature for centuries, precisely because it cannot simply be pointed at.

You may also hear the word used in the context of art. Abstract art is art that does not attempt to depict or represent recognisable real-world objects, people, or scenes. Instead, it uses shapes, colours, lines, and forms to express ideas, emotions, or purely aesthetic experiences. When you look at an abstract painting, you might not be able to say "that is a tree" or "that is a face" — and that is the point. The artist is working directly with concepts or feelings rather than with realistic images of physical things. The word carries the same core meaning: removed from the concrete, physical world and operating at the level of idea or feeling.

When someone says a person is good at "abstract thinking," they mean that person is able to reason about concepts and ideas beyond specific, concrete examples. A child who can only understand "3" by counting three actual physical objects is thinking concretely. A person who understands "3" as a general, universal concept that applies to anything — and can manipulate it in their mind without needing physical objects — is thinking abstractly. Abstract thinking allows you to generalise, to spot patterns across different situations, to understand principles, and to reason about things you cannot directly observe.

Many people assume that because something is abstract, it must be vague, unimportant, or impractical. This is wrong. Abstract concepts are among the most powerful and consequential things humans deal with. Wars have been fought over abstract ideas like freedom and justice. Civilisations are built on abstract concepts like law, rights, and morality. Mathematics — almost entirely abstract — is the foundation of all modern science and technology. The fact that something is abstract simply means it exists as an idea rather than a physical object. It says nothing about whether it is important, meaningful, or real.

So, when you see the word "abstract" used as an adjective, ask yourself: can this thing be physically touched, seen, or directly experienced through the senses? If yes, it leans concrete. If no — if it exists primarily as a concept, idea, principle, or quality in the mind — it is abstract. The more removed something is from any specific, physical, sensory reality, the more abstract it is. And the more it deals with pure thought, general principles, or invisible qualities, the deeper into abstraction it goes.
